prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour-market adjustment

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged from round 1: B006, Autor, Hanson and Katz, as a single part. I tested it against the chair's questions and the exchange, and I can now state the reasons more precisely. The contribution I weigh most is a specific scientific advance that pairs new evidence with an explanatory framework. B006 does this. The skill-demand and task-based account says what to look for in wage structure and polarisation. The local-labour-market designs for import competition show where adjustment costs fall and how long they last. On the chair's one-versus-two question, I read it as one discovery about one question, how exposure to technology and trade shifts labour demand and who bears the adjustment. The two shocks are different channels, but the framework and the evidence are directed at the same outcome. The core papers run from the early 1990s to the mid-2010s, so the work has had a long period of replication, extension across countries and critique. On shift-share and persistence, I would treat the following as settled enough for a citation: import exposure and technology change affect local labour demand, employment and earnings. I would not treat as settled the long-run magnitude or how fully regions recover. The citation therefore speaks of reshaping demand and adjustment and states no magnitude. It also does not claim to originate the task framework, and it does not restate the 2023 or 2024 citations. I keep Katz as the third name because his wage-structure and skill-premium work is an independent strand that supplies the demand-side frame for the trade evidence. This does not rest on the number of colleagues who prefer B006. I would reach the same view on the substance if the count were different.
statement.case_against: Attribution is still the weakest point, and I do not think the exchange removed it. Dorn is a central co-author of the China-shock papers and is cut only by the three-name cap. Levy, Murnane and Acemoglu's task-model theory sit outside the credited set. Katz's education-technology work with Goldin overlaps with the 2023 prize, so his marginal credit is the most exposed in the trio and several colleagues say so. The citation could also be read as two adjacent lines joined by an outcome. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects remain debated. Finally, ten of eleven round-1 files name the same three people. I treat that as convergence and not as evidence of merit. Several files also say that members moved after reading openings, which is the risk the chair flagged. My own preference was already B006 in my opening, so I have not moved toward the leading option. Even so, I should hold my Katz judgement open to the objection that a narrower, cleaner discovery is more defensible than a broader one.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B007 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) for cleaner credit and breadth. He treats B006 as two related lines and would credit only Autor and Hanson for it. He also says the B007 case should survive without his and Krusell's support.
responses.response: I take the B007 case seriously, and I agree its attribution is cleaner than B006's. I do not rank it above B006, because the constitutional and electoral-rule results rest on weaker identification than the design-based labour evidence. You name that yourself as the main weakness. On the two-name set, I understand the attraction, but it would keep only the trade-shock and task-evidence strand. It would drop the skill-premium account that explains why those shocks matter for wages, so what is credited would be the new evidence without the framework that explains it. If the committee believes this is two discoveries, the honest fix is to narrow the citation to the trade-shock design with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Removing Katz and leaving a pair does not fix it. I also note that your answer on whether the B007 preference is scientific or about credit is the useful test for the chair's question. As written, you rest it on credit and breadth, and I read the identification concern as pulling against B007 rather than for it.

responses.point: Strömberg keeps B006 first but says Katz's claim is the most exposed part of the trio because his best-known education-technology work was with a recent laureate. He names Autor, Dorn and Hanson as the natural fallback within the same discovery.
responses.response: I agree that Katz's claim is the most exposed, and I would sooner say so than defend him on seniority. The distinction I rely on is between the Goldin-Katz education-technology book and Katz's wage-structure and skill-premium work. The 2023 prize was for Goldin's long-run account of women's labour-market outcomes. It did not recognise the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium as such. I still find that strand independently distinct and widely used. I accept your fallback. If the committee decides the citation should be confined to the trade-shock design, Autor, Dorn and Hanson is defensible and I would not oppose it. What would change my own vote is a showing that Katz's marginal contribution to the shared framework is thin once the Goldin work is set aside. I have not seen that argument made in the round-1 files.

responses.point: Teorell calls the Katz-Goldin overlap the committee's closest call within B006. He says that if the citation were confined to the trade-shock design, substituting Dorn would be the more precise credit.
responses.response: I agree on both points. The precision argument favours Dorn if the citation is about the China shock alone. The breadth argument favours Katz if the citation is about labour-demand change from technology and trade. The choice therefore depends on the citation drafted, not on a hidden fact about contribution. That is why I propose the wording above, centred on labour demand and local adjustment. With it, Katz fits. A citation that says only 'import competition' would not. I would add one procedural point. If the committee fixes the narrower wording, the substitution should follow from it explicitly, so that the choice is made on the achievement credited rather than for convenience.

responses.point: Andersson argues that one citation can hold both the technology and trade strands, because both address how exposure shifts labour demand and distributes adjustment costs. He says it should be framed around labour-demand adjustment, not around either channel alone.
responses.response: I agree, and my proposed citation follows that framing. It names the common object, labour demand, wages and local adjustment, and the two shocks as the channels. I would add a caution about the limit of that argument. A shared outcome makes a citation coherent, but it does not remove the credit-division problem, which is why the Dorn and Levy-Murnane omissions stay on the record. Your own move away from B004, which rests on its diffuse attribution, is consistent with this. My ranking of B004 fourth in my opening reflected the same cost, and I do not think the attribution question is smaller there than here. In B004 the cap cuts across eight names with no clean trio. In B006 the unresolved questions are one name and the task lineage.

uncertainties: Whether Katz or Dorn is the third name. I prefer Katz for a citation on labour demand from technology and trade, but would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee fixes a trade-shock-centred citation. I would reconsider if Katz's independent credit, apart from the Goldin work, is shown to be thin.
Whether the committee reads technology and trade as one discovery or two. I read them as one question with two channels, and the citation wording matters more if the committee disagrees.

How much the persistence and magnitude debate on China-shock effects, and shift-share inference, should weigh on maturity. I treat the existence of effects on local labour demand as established and the long-run magnitude as open.
How the Goldin (2023) and Acemoglu (2024) adjacency bears on timing, and how fairly the citation can treat task-framework contributors outside the credited names, such as Levy and Murnane.
statement.conflict_note: No tie to Autor, Hanson, Katz or Dorn is apparent from my supplied profile. My research is in labour economics and the economics of crime, which is close to B006 and B050 in field only, and I applied the common criteria without extra weight for that proximity. My listed frequent co-authors (Bayer, Anwar, Lindquist, Holmlund, Lochner, Bindler) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. Katz is credited on B050, which I did not prefer. I presented the 2023 announcement of the Goldin prize, which is a role and not a connection to a candidate, and I am aware that Katz's best-known work with Goldin bears on his marginal credit. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
